title: Malachi 3:13–18
context: The LORD says, “Your words have been harsh against me,” and the disputation continues with “Yet you say” as the people ask, “What have we spoken against you?” They have said that it is vain to serve God and that the proud prosper, but then “those who feared the LORD spoke one with another,” and the LORD heard, and “a book of memory was written before him,” with the promise that they will be his own possession and that one day the difference between the righteous and the wicked will be seen. Both traditions read the passage as shared ground about God’s attention to the faithful who are discouraged (cf. Ps 73:3, 13), and questions about God’s books and final perseverance point to the existing boxes at Exodus 32:33 and Revelation 3:5.

verses.text: “Your words have been harsh against me,” says the LORD. “Yet you say, ‘What have we spoken against you?’
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD says, “Your words have been harsh against me,” and the people answer, “What have we spoken against you?” Arminian readers note the disputation form again.

The people do not recognize their own complaint.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see hearts unaware of their hardness toward God.

Shared ground: both traditions read the exchange as the setting for what the people have been saying, which the next verses quote.

verses.text: You have said, ‘It is vain to serve God,’ and ‘What profit is it that we have followed his instructions and that we have walked mournfully before the LORD of Armies?
verses.arminianNotes:
The people have said, “It is vain to serve God,” and asked what profit there is in obedience. Arminian readers note the discouragement behind the words.

They felt their mourning before God brought no reward.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise hear a complaint like Psalm 73:13.

Shared ground: both traditions read the words as real struggle among God’s people, which the LORD answers with judgment and remembrance rather than silence.

verses.text: Now we call the proud happy; yes, those who work wickedness are built up; yes, they tempt God, and escape.’
verses.arminianNotes:
The people continue, “Now we call the proud happy; yes, those who work wickedness are built up.” Arminian readers note that the prosperity of the wicked troubles them.

The same struggle appears in Psalm 73:3, 12.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the question of God’s justice pressed hard.

Shared ground: both traditions agree that the complaint is honest about appearances, and that the following verses give the LORD’s answer.

verses.text: Then those who feared the LORD spoke one with another; and the LORD listened and heard, and a book of memory was written before him for those who feared the LORD and who honored his name.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Then those who feared the LORD spoke one with another; and the LORD listened and heard, and a book of memory was written before him.” Arminian readers note the faithful encouraging each other.

God notices and remembers them.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise take comfort that God keeps record of those who honor his name.

Shared ground: both traditions rejoice in God’s attention to the faithful, and questions about books and perseverance are treated in the existing boxes at Exodus 32:33 and Revelation 3:5.

verses.text: They shall be mine,” says the LORD of Armies, “my own possession in the day that I make. I will spare them, as a man spares his own son who serves him.
verses.arminianNotes:
“They shall be mine,” says the LORD of Armies, “my own possession in the day that I make.” Arminian readers note the tender promise of belonging.

God will spare them “as a man spares his own son who serves him.”
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise hear God claiming his people as his treasured possession (cf. Exod 19:5).

Shared ground: both traditions agree that the promise is a comfort to those who fear the LORD, and both read the father-son image as care rather than reward earned.

verses.text: Then you shall return and discern between the righteous and the wicked, between him who serves God and him who doesn’t serve him.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Then you shall return and discern between the righteous and the wicked, between him who serves God and him who doesn’t serve him.” Arminian readers note that the complaint of 3:14–15 will be answered.

The difference will become plain.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see God’s justice made visible in his time.

Shared ground: both traditions agree that what is hidden now will be revealed, and that serving God is not in vain.
